aiCheat.title: Working with AI cheat sheet
aiCheat.intro: What to check in an AI pull request, chapter by chapter, and how to ask for the fix. Filter, click a line to copy it, or jump to the level that practises it.

edges.title: Try the edge you were given
edges.summary: Assistants get the middle right and the edges wrong. Put the number from the ask through every comparison: 11 in the basket, then 12.

examples.0: with 11 in the basket: is 11 < 11 true?

names.title: Check what each name holds
names.summary: A variable that holds almost the right thing reads fine. Follow each value to where it comes from.

examples.0: the whole basket's count, used for one line

conditions.title: Read a condition both ways
conditions.summary: Say out loud when it is true, and what happens then: a show-condition assigned to hidden hides exactly the wrong time.

examples.0: true from 20 € on, and that hides the coffee

cases.title: Follow a new value everywhere
cases.summary: A new option, size or method has to reach every switch and lookup that knows the old ones. Search the diff for where it ends up.

examples.0: is there a case for the new value?

units.title: Keep every number with its unit
units.summary: Percent or share, euros or cents, whole euros or to the cent: put a real number through each line, unit and all.

examples.0: 10 is a percentage here, not a share
examples.1: whole euros, where the cent was asked for

every-claim.title: Hold each claim against the code
every-claim.summary: Every line of the description is a promise. Find the code that keeps it, and try the case it names.

examples.0: “handles an empty basket”: what is 0 / 0?

no-change.title: “No behaviour change” is a claim too
no-change.summary: A refactor that sorts in place, caches or reorders changes behaviour. Compare what main does with what this does, not how it reads.

examples.0: sort changes the list it is called on

linked.title: Read the issue it says it fixes
linked.summary: “Fixes #142” is checked against the issue, not the title: does the change fix what the issue asks for, or another symptom?

a-check.title: A test needs a check
a-check.summary: A test without a matcher passes whatever the code does. Count the checks, and ask what would make the test fail.

examples.0: no matcher: this checks nothing

mocked.title: Don't mock what you test
mocked.summary: A mock of the function under test returns what the test says, so the test checks the mock.

examples.0: the test now checks its own return value

on-main.title: Run the tests on main too
on-main.summary: A test that passes on main as well doesn't check the change; one bent to the bug fails on main and shows the right value.

edge-tests.title: Coverage isn't the edge
edge-tests.summary: Every line ran, and the case that breaks it never did. Test the inputs that round, split unevenly or come out empty.

examples.0: rounded per share: 6.50 € between three is 6.51 €

run-it.title: Run it: the Console names what isn't there
run-it.summary: A made-up method, export or removed property fails at once, in so many words. Look the real one up before you trust the call.

examples.0: arrays have no last()

options.title: An unknown option is ignored quietly
options.summary: Intl and most APIs ignore an option they don't know: no error, no change. Check the option's name in the documentation.

examples.0: no such option: the real one is trailingZeroDisplay

packages.title: Check a package exists before you install it
packages.summary: An assistant can name a package that doesn't exist, and anyone can publish one under that name. Look it up on the registry first.

examples.0: a package nobody published (yet)

as-text.title: Text from outside goes in as text
as-text.summary: A review, a note or a name put in with innerHTML is markup, and markup can run script. Use textContent; escaping by list always misses something.

examples.0: the review's text becomes HTML

secrets.title: Anything the browser gets is public
secrets.summary: A secret key in a page's file is everyone's key. It belongs on the server, read from its environment, and a leaked one gets rotated. Publishable keys are the exception their provider names.

who.title: Check who may, on the server
who.summary: Hiding a button is manners, not security. Every route checks who is calling, and whose thing it is.

examples.0: this route checks staff; does the new one?

trust.title: The server decides what only it may
trust.summary: Prices, totals and redirects that come in the request are the customer's to change. The server works them out itself.

examples.0: the total, as the customer's browser sent it

size.title: Size the diff against the ask
size.summary: One word asked for, forty lines changed: something else is in there. A reformat or a rewrite hides what really changed.

side.title: Changes on the side come out
side.summary: A helper swapped, a feature nobody asked for: each is its own decision and its own pull request.

rewrite.title: Read a rewrite's removed lines as a checklist
rewrite.summary: When a line would do and a rewrite came, check that everything the old code did is still done.

two.title: One pull request, one change
two.summary: A rename with a new rule inside is two changes: the rule needs its own review, and its own pull request.

name-kind.title: Name the kind: it is the instruction
name-kind.summary: An assistant does what your comment says the problem is. Bug: change the code. Missing test: add a check. Invented API: use the real one. Security: move it where it is safe. Scope: take it out.

real-check.title: Ask for the check, not a fix
real-check.summary: When the code is right and the test checks nothing, say the test is missing: called a bug, the code gets changed or the test gets a check that checks nothing.

examples.0: the check the test was missing

not-caught.title: Look it up, don't catch it
not-caught.summary: Called a bug, an invented call gets a try around it: the error is gone, and so is the evidence. Name the API that isn't there.

examples.0: the real way to the last item

not-hidden.title: Hidden is not private
not-hidden.summary: A secret split into pieces or marked with a comment still goes to every browser. Ask for it to move, not to be hidden.

examples.0: where the key belongs: the server's environment

out.title: An extra comes out
out.summary: Called a bug, an extra gets repaired and stays, often with a rule of its own. Scope asks for it to come out.

fine-code.title: Flag only what is wrong
fine-code.summary: A comment on fine code is an instruction too: the assistant changes it, and the change is the new bug.

examples.0: right as it is: flagged, it gets “fixed” the wrong way

commit.title: Review the commit like a new pull request
commit.summary: Read what the commit changed, run it again, and approve only what you would have approved in round 1. A confident reply is not a fix.

webCheat.title: Web fundamentals cheat sheet
webCheat.intro: The browser's rules from every chapter and the messages it shows, in a few lines each. Filter, click a line to copy it, or jump to the level that practises it.

origin.title: Origin
origin.summary: An origin is scheme, host and port together. Two addresses are the same origin only when all three match; a subdomain, www or another port is another origin. A page may send requests anywhere, but reads another origin's answer only when that server allows it.

examples.0: The shop's page
examples.1: Its API: another origin
examples.2: www is another host, so another origin
examples.3: Another port, another origin

allow-origin.title: Access-Control-Allow-Origin
allow-origin.summary: The server's word that a page from that origin may read its answer. The browser checks it, the server just answers: without it the request still arrives and runs, and the page gets "Failed to fetch". Fix it on the server, never in the page (no-cors only gets an answer nobody can read).

examples.0: The shop's page may read it
examples.1: Any page may read it (only without credentials)

preflight.title: Preflight
preflight.summary: A request that a plain form couldn't send (application/json, a header of the page's own, DELETE, PUT, PATCH) asks first: an OPTIONS request with Access-Control-Request-Method and -Headers. The real request goes out only when that answer allows it; refused, server.js sees the OPTIONS and nothing else.

examples.0: A route for the preflight of the path the page calls
examples.1: The page's origin, as on the real answer
examples.2: Name the headers the page sets
examples.3: Answer with no body

credentials.title: Credentials
credentials.summary: With credentials (cookies) the answer is about one customer, so the star is never enough: the server names the page's exact origin and sends Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Echo an Origin back only after checking it against a list of exact origins, and add Vary: Origin.

examples.0: The page sends its cookies along
examples.1: Exactly the word true
examples.2: Echo an origin only from a list of exact ones

allow-headers.title: Allow-Headers and Allow-Methods
allow-headers.summary: Every header the page sets itself (Authorization, X-Basket-Id) and every method but GET, HEAD and POST must be named in the preflight's answer. With credentials the star is just a name and allows nothing.

examples.0: Each header of the page's own, by name (any case)
examples.1: Methods beyond GET, HEAD and POST, as written

not-browsers.title: curl is not a browser
not-browsers.summary: curl, Postman and other servers send what you type and read every answer: there is no page to protect, so no CORS. A curl test proves nothing about the page, and CORS protects no route: anything that isn't a browser can still send the request, so the route checks who may do what.

session-cookie.title: A session cookie
session-cookie.summary: HttpOnly keeps it from scripts, Secure keeps it on https, SameSite=Lax keeps it from other sites' requests but a link, and Path=/ sends it to every address. res.cookie writes Path=/ for you; a line written by hand has to say it.

examples.0: Express writes the line for you, Path=/ included
examples.1: The same cookie written by hand: then Path=/ has to be there

same-site.title: SameSite
same-site.summary: Which requests started by another site carry the cookie. Lax is what sessions want; Strict breaks every link from an email; None needs Secure and goes with every site's request (and so with every forged one).

examples.0: Only requests the cookie's own site starts, no links from elsewhere
examples.1: Also a top-level GET from another site (a link); no form POSTs, images or fetches
examples.2: Every request, any site; refused without Secure
examples.3: Chrome treats it as Lax, but sends it with another site's POST for its first two minutes

site.title: Site is not origin
site.summary: SameSite is about sites: the scheme and the registrable domain. api.cornerbakery.shop and cornerbakery.shop are two origins and one site, so a Lax cookie goes with every request between them. CORS is about origins; cookies are about sites.

csrf.title: Cross-site request forgery
csrf.summary: A cookie goes with every request its SameSite allows, whoever starts it: with None, another site's form posts as the customer. CORS plays no part (a form is no fetch). Lax stops it; so does checking the Origin exactly, or a CSRF token. Never a loose check like startsWith or includes.

examples.0: The Origin compared exactly, before doing anything

http-only.title: HttpOnly
http-only.summary: document.cookie shows every script on the page (yours, a widget's, an XSS) every cookie of the host that is not HttpOnly. HttpOnly keeps a session from being read and taken away; a script on the page can still send requests as the customer while she is there.

examples.0: Shows every cookie that is not HttpOnly

path-domain.title: Path and Domain
path-domain.summary: Without Path a cookie gets the folder of the address that set it (/auth for /auth/login) and goes only below it. Without Domain it goes to its own host only; with one, to every host under that domain. Neither is a wall against scripts.

examples.0: Every address of the host
examples.1: Every host under cornerbakery.shop

where-token.title: Where a token lives
where-token.summary: Every script on the page reads localStorage and sessionStorage, and a Bearer token works for whoever sends it, from any machine. An HttpOnly cookie is the one place no script reaches; then it needs SameSite, as chapter 2 showed.

examples.0: server.js reads the session from the cookie
examples.1: The page sends the cookie with every API call

text-as-text.title: Text stays text
text-as-text.summary: innerHTML turns a review into elements, and an image's onerror runs as the page's own code (cross-site scripting). textContent never makes an element. Stripping script tags with a regex misses the next spelling; a Content-Security-Policy is a second wall, not a replacement.

examples.0: One element per review
examples.1: Its text shown as written, angle brackets and all

expiry.title: A token that ends
expiry.summary: A cookie's Max-Age only tells one browser when to forget it; a copy lives until the token itself ends. expiresIn writes exp into the token and jwt.verify refuses it from then on. jwt.decode checks nothing, a signature proves who made a token, not until when.

examples.0: A token that ends after 15 minutes
examples.1: Checks the signature and exp; decode checks neither

refresh.title: Refresh
refresh.summary: A short session and a long refresh token that only goes to /auth, HttpOnly, each one used once. The browser renews nothing itself: the page's api helper, on a 401, refreshes once and sends the same request again; when the refresh fails too, it hands back the 401.

examples.0: Keep the request as a function, to send it again
examples.1: Trade the refresh token for a new session

sign-out.title: Signing out
sign-out.summary: clearCookie only asks one browser to forget. A copy works for as long as the server accepts it, so sign-out ends the session where it is checked: the refresh token deleted, the session token refused until it would run out anyway. Only that customer's session, nobody else's.

examples.0: Above the sign-out route: the sessions that ended
examples.1: In the route: this session ends
examples.2: In the route: its refresh token can't renew anything
examples.3: In customerOf, before its return: an ended session is nobody

cache-control.title: Cache-Control
cache-control.summary: How long an answer stays right, said where it is made: on the server. Within its max-age the browser doesn't ask at all; no-cache keeps a copy and asks every time; no-store keeps nothing; private keeps it out of shared caches.

examples.0: Use the copy for an hour without asking
examples.1: Keep a copy, ask before every use
examples.2: Keep no copy: the whole answer every time
examples.3: Only the customer's own browser may keep it
examples.4: Any cache may hand it to anyone for a minute: never for one customer's answer

revalidate.title: Asking with an ETag
revalidate.summary: With no-cache the browser sends its copy's ETag as If-None-Match. Express makes the ETag from the body: unchanged, it answers 304 with no body and the copy is used; changed, the new answer comes in full. An ETag that never changes keeps old prices forever.

examples.0: Never stale, and cheap while nothing changed

cache-rows.title: Cache rows in Network
cache-rows.summary: How the Network panel shows where an answer came from.

examples.0: No request at all: the browser used its fresh copy
examples.1: Asked, nothing changed: no body, the copy is used
examples.2: A whole answer from the server

shared-cache.title: Shared caches
shared-cache.summary: A CDN keeps one copy per address (and per header Vary names), never per person, and hands it to whoever asks next. An answer that depends on the cookie says private or no-store, its errors too; a unique address only hides it.

examples.0: Only her browser keeps the account

vary.title: Vary
vary.summary: Names the request headers an answer depends on, so a cache keeps one copy per value. An answer whose Allow-Origin depends on the Origin needs Vary: Origin on every answer of the route, or one page gets another page's copy.

examples.0: One copy per Origin

new-address.title: A copy you can't take back
new-address.summary: A copy stays fresh for the max-age it came with, whatever the server says now: only an address the browser has no copy of reaches it (a versioned file name, a new query), or a page that asks to revalidate. Long max-age belongs to addresses whose content never changes.

examples.0: An address her browser has no copy of
examples.1: This request asks the server first

order.title: What runs when
order.summary: One task at a time, each to its end. After every task all microtasks run, also the ones they queue. Between two tasks, when a frame is due (about every 16 ms), the browser may render: requestAnimationFrame callbacks, style, layout, paint.

examples.0: 1. Runs now, to the end of the task
examples.1: 2. Microtasks: all of them, before anything else
examples.2: 3. Other tasks, one at a time: a 0 ms timer usually runs before the next frame
examples.3: 4. When a frame is due, between two tasks: then style, layout and paint

paint-first.title: Paint before long work
paint-first.summary: The browser renders only between tasks, so what a task shows and hides again is never painted. Let a frame in first: wait for its callbacks, then for a task after it. setTimeout alone usually comes before the frame, and await Promise.resolve() never leaves the task.

examples.0: Waits until the frame with the spinner is painted

dispatch.title: A tap and its listeners
dispatch.summary: For a real tap the browser runs the microtasks after each listener, before the next one; element.click() from code runs every listener first. A test that clicks from code can pass where a tap fails. A listener on the document hears every tap that bubbles up.

examples.0: The closing listener ignores the toggle's own taps
examples.1: Or the toggle's listener stops its tap from bubbling up, before its await

forced-layout.title: Forced layout
forced-layout.summary: Reading a size or position (scrollHeight, offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect) after changing the page makes the browser lay it out at once. Write everything, then read once; a loop that writes and reads in turn lays the page out every time.

examples.0: Once, after all the rows are in
examples.1: Or build the rows off the page and add them at once

transition.title: A transition needs a before
transition.summary: A transition runs between two styles the browser computed. An element added and changed in the same task has only one. Two frames give it a before; so does reading its computed style first. A single requestAnimationFrame is the classic miss.

examples.0: The class added two frames later
examples.1: Forces the style (not a layout), which is enough

yield.title: Break up long work
yield.summary: Microtasks never let a frame in: a loop of await Promise.resolve() runs to its end in one checkpoint and the page paints once, at the end. Awaiting a task (a timer, a message) or a frame lets the browser render in between.

examples.0: A real break: a frame may come in
examples.1: One chunk per frame

name.title: Accessible name
name.summary: What a reader says a control is called: aria-labelledby, then aria-label, then the label or alt, then the content, last a title. An icon hidden with aria-hidden gives none. The name should say which one it is, not just what it does.

examples.0: A name that says which product
examples.1: Or text for readers, hidden on screen (the class is in style.css)
examples.2: Hides the icon from readers: then the button needs a name

button.title: Use a button
button.summary: A button is in the Tab order, has a role and clicks on Enter and on Space, so its click listener runs for the keyboard too. A div with a click listener is for the mouse only; rebuilding it takes role, tabindex and a keydown handler, all three.

examples.0: Tab, role and keys for free

keys.title: Keys
keys.summary: What the keyboard does in the levels, as browsers do it.

examples.0: Next or previous control in page order
examples.1: Clicks a button, follows a link
examples.2: Clicks a button; on a link it scrolls the page
examples.3: Closes a dialog when its code says so (showModal does it itself)

expanded.title: Open or closed
expanded.summary: A reader knows a button opens something only from aria-expanded, kept in step with what is shown in the one place it is shown or hidden. A details element with a summary does it all natively. A label that changes is a new name, not a state.

examples.0: Closed at the start
examples.1: In the one place the list is shown or hidden
examples.2: Instead of the button: details wraps the list, summary is its button, no script at all

live.title: Live regions
live.summary: A reader hears a change only in a live region that was on the page, live and shown, before the change, or where focus goes. Keep an empty region in the markup and write into it; clearing it first lets the same message be said again.

examples.0: There from the start, filled when the address is wrong
examples.1: Polite: said when the reader is done
examples.2: Or focus the field and point it at its error

focus.title: Where focus goes
focus.summary: When the focused element disappears, focus falls back to the page. The code that hides a dialog puts focus back on the button that opened it, on every way out. showModal does all of it, and keeps Tab inside; aria-modal alone keeps nobody in.

examples.0: Back to the button that opened the dialog
examples.1: On a dialog element (not a div): focus in, page inert, Escape, focus back

inline.title: Inline code
inline.summary: A Content-Security-Policy can't tell the page's inline code from an attacker's: unsafe-inline allows every inline handler and script. Move the page's own code into files, list where scripts may come from, and everything inline is refused.

examples.0: Scripts only from the shop and the widget, nothing inline
examples.1: The handler in app.js instead of onclick in the markup

framing.title: Who may frame the page
framing.summary: Any site may show any page in a frame unless the page says who may; a see-through frame turns a click on the bait into a click on the page. frame-ancestors lists exactly who; X-Frame-Options is the older header, without a list. Neither works in a meta tag.

examples.0: The shop itself and the market, nobody else
examples.1: Nobody at all, the market too (ignored once frame-ancestors is there)

fetch-directives.title: Where the page may send
fetch-directives.summary: script-src decides which scripts run; connect-src where they may send requests, img-src where images come from. Without them, or default-src, a script the policy let in may send what it reads anywhere. A directive of its own replaces default-src for that kind.

examples.0: The shop by default, scripts and requests to the widget and the stats

report-only.title: Report-only
report-only.summary: Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only is a dry run: each violation goes to the Console (as info) and to report-uri, and the code runs anyway. Fix what the reports name on the page's side, then send the same policy as Content-Security-Policy. It has no meta-tag form.

examples.0: Watch: reports, refuses nothing
examples.1: Enforce: the same policy, now it refuses

strict.title: A strict policy
strict.summary: An allowlist trusts addresses, and a big CDN serves anyone's files. A nonce the server makes fresh for every page, on the page's own tags, trusts the tags instead; strict-dynamic passes that trust to the scripts they add and ignores addresses. A nonce that never changes is no nonce.

examples.0: A fresh nonce for every page
examples.1: The policy with that nonce; Google's recommended one adds object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none'
examples.2: The page's own tags carry it (server.js puts the nonce in for the marker)

more-headers.title: More headers
more-headers.summary: Two more a shop sends on every answer: nosniff runs a script only when it is served as JavaScript, and Referrer-Policy decides how much of the page's address other sites see.

examples.0: A text file is never run as a script
examples.1: Other sites see only the origin (the default)

no-allow-origin.means: The server answered, but didn't say your page may read it. Fixed on that server, or by calling your own origin, never in the page.
no-allow-origin.look: The origin the message names, then the server's answer headers in Network.

failed-fetch.means: The browser kept the answer from the page, or never sent the request: CORS, a policy, or no network. The reason is in another Console line.
failed-fetch.look: The Console line before it, and the request's row in Network.

preflight.means: The request asked first (OPTIONS), and that answer didn't allow it; the real request was never sent.
preflight.look: The OPTIONS row in Network and in the Server panel: is there a route that answers it?

wildcard.means: The request sends cookies, and the star doesn't cover that: the server has to name the page's origin and allow credentials.
wildcard.look: Access-Control-Allow-Origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials in the answer.

header-not-allowed.means: The page sets a header of its own, and the preflight's answer doesn't name it.
header-not-allowed.look: Access-Control-Allow-Headers in the OPTIONS answer, against the headers the page sets.

method-not-allowed.means: The method needs a yes from the preflight, and Access-Control-Allow-Methods doesn't list it.

none-insecure.means: The browser refused to store the cookie: SameSite=None needs Secure too. Usually the fix is Lax, not Secure.
none-insecure.look: The answer's Set-Cookie under Cookies, in the request's details in Network.

lax-blocked.means: Another site started the request and it was no link, so the Lax cookie stayed home: the protection working.
lax-blocked.look: Where the request came from (From in the request's details in Network), and whether it should carry the cookie at all.

not-on-path.means: The cookie belongs to another path, usually the folder of the address that set it.
not-on-path.look: The cookie's Path in Application, against the request's address.

strict-blocked.means: A link from another site (an email) carries no Strict cookie, so the page looks signed out until a reload.
strict-blocked.look: The cookie's SameSite in Application; a session wants Lax.

inline-handler.means: An onclick, onerror or other handler in the markup was refused by the policy, the page's own or an attacker's.
inline-handler.look: Where the handler comes from: move the page's own into app.js with addEventListener.

script-src.means: A script from an address the policy doesn't list was refused before it ran.
script-src.look: Whether you meant that script: if so, add its address to the policy; if not, nothing to fix.

framing.means: The page's frame-ancestors doesn't list the site that framed it, so the frame stays empty. Shown in the framing site's Console.
framing.look: The frame-ancestors list in the framed page's answer.

x-frame-options.means: The page's X-Frame-Options refuses to be framed there. DENY refuses everyone; SAMEORIGIN everyone but itself.
x-frame-options.look: The framed page's answer headers; frame-ancestors can list exactly who may.

connect-src.means: A script asked to send a request to an address the policy's connect-src (or default-src) doesn't list; the request never left.
connect-src.look: Which script sent it, and whether that address belongs on the list.

report-only.means: The report-only policy would refuse this, but only reports it: the code ran.
report-only.look: Fix what it names on the page's side, then send the policy as Content-Security-Policy.

nosniff.means: nosniff is on and the file isn't served as JavaScript, so the browser won't run it as a script.
nosniff.look: The file's Content-Type in Network: serve scripts as text/javascript.

debugCheat.title: Debugging cheat sheet
debugCheat.intro: Every panel and the error messages from the levels, in a few lines each. Filter, click an example to copy it, or jump to the level that practises it.

read-trace.title: Read an error and its stack
read-trace.summary: The first line says what went wrong, the frames under it say where. The top frame is the line that threw; each frame below it is the line that called the one above. Start at the top, and if that code has always worked, step down to the call that handed it a wrong value. A link or frame opens its line in Code. A button that "does nothing" has usually thrown here: errors go to the Console, not to the page.

syntax.title: Syntax errors and the blank page
syntax.summary: A syntax error is found before any code runs, so no line of that module (or of any module that imports it) runs: the page is blank. It has no frames, only where the browser gave up, which is usually after the real mistake. Read the lines above it for a missing bracket; the indentation often gives it away.

input.title: The input line
input.summary: Type an expression at the bottom of the Console and press Enter: it runs inside the app. › is your input, ← the value as a one-line preview, and an error shows in red. Up and Down bring back your earlier inputs. Clear empties the Console, and so does a Reload. Look at the value first, then find out where it came from.

examples.0: What is it? A function, or an object that holds formatPrice and toCents?
examples.1: The type of a value
examples.2: Are two lines one object? true means one object under two names

await.title: Top-level await
await.summary: The input line accepts await, so you can see what a promise settles to without writing an async function. A rejection shows in red. const x = await … defines x for your later inputs.

examples.0: The price once the promise settles
examples.1: Without await you only see a Promise, not its value
examples.2: Keep the result for later inputs (it becomes a property of the window)

log.title: Log what you do not expect
log.summary: A catch that only says "failed" throws the real error away, and the Console stays quiet. Log it, or handle only the failures you know.

examples.0: Show the real error from a catch
examples.1: Label a value so you can find it in the Console

status.title: Status codes
status.summary: A status says whether the server understood the request. 2xx worked, 4xx means the request was wrong, 5xx means the server failed. The Network panel colours 2xx green and 4xx and 5xx red. Read the response body: the server often says what went wrong.

examples.0: Worked
examples.1: Saved a new thing (a POST). It can still have saved the wrong data
examples.2: The server refused what you sent: read its message in the response body
examples.3: Nothing lives at that address: the path is wrong
examples.4: The request clashes with the current state (the oven is already full)
examples.5: It arrived, but a field is not valid (a total that is not a number)
examples.6: The server crashed on it: look in its Logs
examples.7: The server cannot answer right now: try again later

no-code.title: Status words without a code
no-code.summary: When there is no answer the page can read, the Network panel shows a word instead of a code. The Console line above or below it says why.

examples.0: The request is still on its way
examples.1: The browser refused to let the page read the answer: the server sent no permission
examples.2: No answer at all (no connection); fetch rejects with "Failed to fetch"
examples.3: The page cancelled it, for example with controller.abort()

details.title: Request and response
details.summary: The panel lists requests in the order sent: method, name, status, time. Select one for its URL, Status, Time, Sent from (opens the line that sent it), and the headers and body of the Request and of the Response. Compare what the page sent with what the server built from it, and with the API description (api.md).

address.title: A 404 is a wrong address
address.summary: fetch does not fail on a 404: the server did answer. Compare the path in the Network panel with the paths the API really has, then follow it back (Sent from) to the line that builds the address.

examples.0: The path the API lists, not the old one

ok.title: Check response.ok
ok.summary: fetch rejects only when no answer arrives. A 404 or a 500 is an answer, so the promise resolves and response.ok is false. Check it right after the fetch, before you read the body as a success.

examples.0: Handle a failed answer before anything else
examples.1: Or look at the code itself

payload.title: Check the payload
payload.summary: When data arrives wrong, look at the request body in the Network panel first: it tells you whether the page sent the wrong thing or the server read it wrong. JSON keeps types: "3" and 3 are different for the server, and a field the server does not know is usually ignored without a word.

examples.0: Form fields give text: send a number as a number

cors.title: CORS
cors.summary: A page may send a request to another origin, but may read the answer only if that server allows it. Without an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header for the page's origin (or *), the browser hides the answer and fetch fails with "Failed to fetch"; the reason is in the Console. It works in curl or Postman because they are not browsers. Fix it on the server, never in the page, or send the call to your own origin, which forwards it.

examples.0: What the other server has to send
examples.1: Same origin: no CORS check at all

double.title: Two POSTs for one click
double.summary: A slow answer invites a second click, and the browser sends what the code says: two clicks, two requests. Ignore clicks while a request is on its way and turn the button back on when the answer is in. This only makes duplicates rarer: a server that takes money also needs a unique id per order (an idempotency key).

examples.0: Ignore clicks while it sends

tree.title: The tree and Refresh
tree.summary: The tree shows the page as markup. It is a snapshot: press Refresh to see the page as it is now. An element without a box is dimmed ("not shown"), and one whose content is wider than its box gets a scroll badge. Keys: Up and Down, Home and End, Right and Left open and close.

styles.title: Matched rules and overridden declarations
styles.summary: Styles lists element.style, then the rules that match from the winner down, each with its media query, its selector, its specificity and where it is written (a link to the line). A declaration struck through lost to a stronger one; one with a warning is refused by the browser. A property that nothing else sets stays active, which is how a price can get bold but not red.

specificity.title: Specificity
specificity.summary: When two rules set the same property, the browser compares selectors: ids first, then classes (and attributes and pseudo-classes), then element names. The panel shows it as ids · classes · types. The order in the file only breaks a tie. Match the specificity or lower the old rule; !important just starts an arms race.

examples.0: 1 · 1 · 0: the id wins over any number of classes
examples.1: 0 · 2 · 0: loses to the rule above, even if it comes later
examples.2: 0 · 2 · 0: ties with the one above, so the later rule wins
examples.3: 0 · 0 · 1: weakest

variables.title: Variables that are not defined
variables.summary: var(--name) with no such property makes the declaration invalid at computed-value time, and the browser reports it nowhere. The property then behaves as if it were not set: a property that is not inherited, like background, gets its starting value (transparent), while an inherited one, like color, takes its parent's value. The panel marks it "--brown is not defined" under the declaration. Look at the :root rule under Inherited from for the real names.

examples.0: An invisible button: the variable does not exist

computed.title: Computed values and contrast
computed.summary: Computed is what the page really gets; the rules show how it got there. It lists display, visibility, opacity, position, z-index, pointer-events, color, background-color, width, height, min-width, overflow, text-overflow and white-space. Invisible is not gone: text and background of the same colour keep their box, so Pick can still select it. Normal text needs a contrast of at least 4.5 : 1.

pick.title: Pick mode
pick.summary: Pick, then click in the app: the element that is really under the pointer is selected (the app never gets that click), the tree opens to it, and hovering outlines it. Escape stops. It shows what a tap lands on, so when a button "does nothing" without an error, pick it: something invisible may sit on top.

covered.title: Something on top of the button
covered.summary: The browser sends a click to the topmost element under the pointer. A transparent box with a higher z-index takes every tap meant for what is below. Let clicks pass through it, or stack or move it differently. Nothing invisible should sit on top of a button.

examples.0: The element ignores the pointer, and so do its children
examples.1: Children that need clicks (a toast) switch it on again
examples.2: Stacked above: check which one has the higher value

box.title: The box and what sticks out
box.summary: Box shows margin, border, padding and content with their sides (a dash for 0), and says "Its content is 512 px wide in a 340 px box: it sticks out." when it does. A flex item will not get narrower than its content unless you allow it, and white-space: nowrap makes that content the whole text.

examples.0: Let a flex item shrink below its content
examples.1: Cut a long text with a "…" (with overflow: hidden and white-space: nowrap)
examples.2: Let a long word or address break

media.title: Media queries
media.summary: A media query is a condition on the width of the page, not on the device. Elements lists only the rules whose query holds right now, and the App shows its width next to the address. Test a layout change at both ends: a phone and a laptop width.

examples.0: Holds from 600 px wide and up: not "on desktop"
examples.1: Holds up to 600 px wide

missing-await.title: Missing await
missing-await.summary: Calling an async function gives you a promise at once, not the result. Written into the page it reads [object Promise]; used as a list it throws "map is not a function" or "is not iterable". await waits for the result: inside an async function, or at the top level of a module. In the Console a promise shows as a Promise, not as its value.

examples.0: Wait for the result
examples.1: Or continue in a then

race.title: Races and AbortController
race.summary: Two requests are on their way and the newer one answers first, so the old answer arrives last and wins. It only happens sometimes. Decide what is still wanted when an answer arrives, or cancel the old request. An aborted fetch rejects with an AbortError (the Network panel says canceled), so catch it and ignore it. A debounce sends fewer requests but does not fix the race.

examples.0: A counter: take a ticket per request
examples.1: Drop the answer when a newer request has started
examples.2: Cancel the old request, if there is one
examples.3: A new controller for the new request
examples.4: Give the request the controller's signal
examples.5: An abort on purpose is not an error

closure.title: Closures and var in a loop
closure.summary: A function made in a loop keeps the variables themselves, not a copy of their values, and reads them when it runs, long after the loop. var belongs to the whole function, so every handler shares one variable and sees the last value. let and const make a fresh one per round.

examples.0: Each round gets its own product
examples.1: Or a callback parameter, which is new for every call

copy.title: Shallow copies
copy.summary: A variable holds a reference to an object, not the object. A spread copies the top level only, so a nested object stays shared and changing one thing changes the other. Check with === in the Console: true means one object. Object.assign is shallow too.

examples.0: Copy everything
examples.1: Copy the nested object as well
examples.2: Or never edit the shared one: replace it

chain.title: Promise chains that lose their value
chain.summary: Each then hands the next one what its callback returns. A callback that returns nothing passes undefined on, and the next one throws. A catch that treats every error as "the server said no" hides the real one. With async and await the code reads top to bottom and nothing can be forgotten between the steps.

examples.0: Return it, or the next then gets undefined
examples.1: The same with await, and one try and catch around it
examples.2: A catch tells you what it does not expect

record.title: Record, then step
record.summary: The Debugger records a run: press Record, use the app, press Stop. The app is never paused: you move through what it already did and see each value as it was then, so you can go back as well as forward. Edited the code? Save, then Record again. A Reload, Reset or Again ends a recording. It opens at the first step a breakpoint stops at.

breakpoints.title: Breakpoints
breakpoints.summary: Click the gutter in Code (Ctrl or Cmd+B, or Breakpoint here in the panel, work without the mouse). Each breakpoint is listed with its line and how often it stopped in the recording ("hit 2 times", "not hit"); a breakpoint that stopped twice for one action shows that something runs twice. Remove it from its list. The breakpoints stay while you are on the page.

condition.title: Conditional breakpoints
condition.summary: Give a breakpoint a condition (the field under it: Enter or leaving it sets it) and it stops only where the condition holds, checked on the values each round had. That finds the one odd row of a thousand. A condition that cannot be read shows why under the field.

examples.0: Stop on the cheap row
examples.1: Stop on the bread with the odd weight
examples.2: Stop on one named item

stepping.title: Step over, into, out and back
stepping.summary: Resume goes to the next breakpoint (with none ahead, to the end). Step over runs the line, Step into goes inside the function it calls, Step out runs to the end of the current function. Step back and Back to the previous breakpoint go the other way. The scrubber shows "Step 37 of 412". Stepping over a line and comparing the Scope before and after shows what it changed.

shortcuts.title: Shortcuts
shortcuts.summary: The keys DevTools uses, while there is a recording and no dialog is open. Step back and Back to the previous breakpoint have no key. Plain F11 stays the browser's full screen.

examples.0: Resume
examples.1: Step over
examples.2: Step into
examples.3: Step out

scope.title: Scope
scope.summary: Scope lists the variables of the current step: Block, Local (with this), Closure and Module. Values look like the browser's preview: strings green, numbers and booleans amber, undefined and null dimmed, functions blue; an object opens. It shows the raw value, with every digit, which is what the code compares: 24.999999999999996 shows as 25.00 on the page. When what the page shows and what the code decides disagree, put a breakpoint where it decides.

stack.title: Call stack
stack.summary: The frames of the current step, top first, each with its function and file:line. Click a frame to see its line in Code and its variables at that moment: the way to find out who called a function, and each time. An "async" line marks the call that started an async function now back from an await.

units.title: Counted, not timed
units.summary: The Performance panel counts: one unit of work is one statement of the app's code that ran (a built-in like sort or toFixed counts as part of the statement that calls it), and request times are the server's scripted delays. The same run shows the same numbers on every computer. Record, use the app, Stop. Show picks the whole recording or one action; the totals are Work, Renders, Requests and Server time.

functions.title: Functions: calls, self and total
functions.summary: Calls is how often a function ran. Self is its own statements, Total is itself and everything it called. A function with a big total and a small self spends its time in what it calls. A huge number of calls of a small function means work inside a loop that does not depend on the round: do it once, outside, or look it up in a Map.

renders.title: Renders and nodes
renders.summary: A render is a call of a function that changed the page; its nodes are the elements and texts it added, removed or changed. One Add should cost the basket a few nodes, not the whole menu 48. Draw again only the part whose data changed (a framework does that bookkeeping for you).

requests.title: Requests over time
requests.summary: Each request has a bar from its start to its end. "Sent once menu answered" marks a waterfall: it waited for another answer though it did not need it. "The same request again" marks an answer that was thrown away. A request per key typed is the third thing to look for.

examples.0: Start them together and wait for all
examples.1: A debounce: each key cancels the timer of the key before
examples.2: A cache by name; keeping the promise also covers a second click

logs.title: Logs
logs.summary: The Logs panel is the server's own story: time on the server's clock, level, route, request id, message and the stack where it failed. Filter by level or by text. A page that shows the server's reference for a failed request (x-request-id) gives you the id to search for; an id of this load links to that request in Network. Compare when the first failure came with when things last worked.

examples.0: Filter on a request id

deploys.title: Deploys and diffs
deploys.summary: Deploys lists the versions newest first: id, who and when, the message, and the live one. "Changes in …" opens the diff per file: added lines green, removed lines red, with their line numbers; a changed line opens in Code. Read the diff for who else uses what changed: damage is often in a file the deploy never touched.

which.title: Which deploy broke it?
which.summary: Put the timeline from the Logs next to the list of deploys: the last good request, the first failure, the deploy in between. With several suspects, bisect: roll back to the middle, check the shop, keep halving.

rollback.title: Roll back
rollback.summary: Roll back to a version sends your saved code back to it (Reload runs it), after asking what changes, which saved changes of your own are replaced and which unsaved edits are dropped. Go back to the last version that worked and no further, then check what it changes and check the shop. Back to live returns to the newest version, and Undo roll back brings your replaced changes back, until you save again. Roll back when you do not know the cause yet or the fix takes longer than customers can wait; with a clear one-line cause, fix forward.

flags.title: Feature flags
flags.summary: A feature flag switches a feature on or off from configuration, so you can turn it off without another deploy. When code behaves differently in one environment, look at the flags it picked: here the deploy named them "live" while the script calls the environment "production", and a fallback quietly handed production the staging flags. Fail loudly instead of falling back.

examples.0: Look up the flags by the environment's name
examples.1: A missing name should stop the page, not hide

json.title: Never build JSON or HTML by hand
json.summary: Gluing text into JSON breaks on exactly the characters JSON gives a meaning to: a quote, a line break, a backslash. Failures that hit only some customers often share such a character: put the failed requests side by side in the Logs. Let JSON.stringify escape it; the same goes for textContent instead of innerHTML. Test with the input real people type.

examples.0: The server reads the note exactly as typed
examples.1: Text stays text in the page

cannot-read.means: The thing before the dot is undefined (or null). The message names what you tried to read, not the mistake, which is a step earlier.
cannot-read.look: The top frame's line and the name just before the dot: often a misspelled property (cart.itmes) or data that has not arrived. Type that name in the Console input.

not-a-function.means: What you called is not a function: an object, undefined, a promise. The function is not missing.
not-a-function.look: Type the name in the Console input and read its value, then check its import: braces take a named export, no braces the default one.

wrong-value.means: A helper got a value of the wrong kind (here the whole cart instead of a number). The helper is usually right.
wrong-value.look: Step down the stack to the frame that called it and see what it passed. Fix it there, not in the helper.

map-not-a-function.means: An array method on something that is not an array. Often a promise, because an await is missing, or an object.
map-not-a-function.look: Type the name in the Console: a Promise instead of the value means a missing await.

not-iterable.means: A for…of, spread or destructuring got something that is not a list: undefined, an object or a promise. In a promise chain, the step before returned nothing.
not-iterable.look: What did the step before return? Each then passes on only what its callback returns.

not-defined.means: No variable of that name is in reach at that line: misspelled, declared in another block (let and const stay between their braces) or never imported.
not-defined.look: Find where it is declared and ask whether that place is in reach of the line in the trace.

before-init.means: A let or const used on a line before the one that declares it.
before-init.look: Move the declaration above its first use.

unexpected-export.means: A syntax error: the browser gave up here, usually a few lines after the real mistake, often a missing bracket. Nothing in that module runs, so the page is blank.
unexpected-export.look: Read the lines above the reported one; look at the indentation for the missing closing brace.

missing-export.means: A named import the module does not export (renamed, or it only has a default export). Nothing in the module graph runs.
missing-export.look: Open the imported file and compare its export names; an import with as keeps the old name in your file.

not-json.means: response.json() got HTML, not JSON: usually the server's error page, because of a wrong address or a server error.
not-json.look: The Network panel: the request's status and the body that came back, before you read any code.

not-found.means: The browser's own line for a failed request. The server answered, but has nothing at that address.
not-found.look: Compare the path with the paths the API lists (api.md); Sent from opens the line that built the address.

failed-fetch.means: No answer the page may read: the browser blocked it (CORS) or there is no connection. It is not an HTTP status.
failed-fetch.look: The line above it in the Console, and the status in Network: CORS error or failed.

cors-blocked.means: The other server did not say your page may read its answer. It is fixed on that server, or by calling your own origin, never in the page.
cors-blocked.look: Which origin and which header the message names; then the request's status (CORS error) in Network.

aborted.means: A fetch was cancelled with controller.abort(): the Network panel says canceled. Expected when you cancel on purpose.
aborted.look: Catch AbortError and ignore it, so the Console only shows real errors.

about.title: Practice the skills you use every day
about.intro: Grindstone is a training ground for developers: short, game-like levels that run in your browser. Four tracks are live: Git, Debugging, Working with AI and Web fundamentals. Git came first, because everyone uses it and almost everyone is a little afraid of rebase.

teammates.title: You are not alone in the repo
teammates.text: Simulated teammates push to origin while you work. Keeping your branch in sync, rebasing onto a moved main and force-pushing safely only make sense when others change things too.

real.title: It feels like the real thing
real.text: Commands and messages follow real git, down to "rejected, fetch first". What you practise here carries over to your own terminal.

graph.title: You see what git does
graph.text: Every command redraws a live commit graph, so branches, merges and rebases stop being invisible.

ide.title: Work the way you work
ide.text: Use a plain terminal, or an IDE layout with files, an editor with conflict actions and a terminal below.

about.how: Everything runs in your browser: Grindstone has its own git simulation in TypeScript, so levels are predictable, undo is instant and what you type never leaves your browser. Debugging levels run a small real app in a sealed frame that can't see Grindstone, your progress or the network. Web fundamentals runs the shop's server.js you edit in that same sealed frame, with the browser's rules modelled, so nothing reaches the network there either. In Working with AI the assistant is scripted: no AI is called, and nothing you write in a review leaves your browser. Your progress stays on your device. To see which levels are too hard, Grindstone counts visits and which levels are started and solved, anonymously and without cookies, on its own server (Umami). If your browser sends Do Not Track, nothing is counted. The code is open source.

performance.label: Performance
performance.intro: Record a run: the app reloads with its code counted, you use it (type in the search, click Add…), then press Stop. Then see how often each function ran and how much work it did, what it changed on the page, and when its requests went out.

performance.recorded: Counted, not timed: one unit of work is one statement of the app's code that ran (a built-in like sort or toFixed counts as part of the statement that calls it), and request times are the server's scripted delays. So the same run shows the same numbers on every computer.

web.a11ySealed: The app runs in a sealed frame: it can't reach Grindstone or your progress. Its accessibility tree comes from your browser's own DOM and styles, read after HTML-AAM and the accessible name spec as Chrome has them; focus, the keyboard and the screen reader are modelled, so every run is the same.
